claims.text: Hyperkalemia: ECG changes are often visible above 5.5 mEq/L. Peaked T waves come first, then a longer PR and a shorter QT.
claims.quote: ECG changes (see figure ECG Patterns in Hyperkalemia ) are frequently visible when serum potassium is > 5.5 mEq/L (> 5.5 mmol/L). Slowing of conduction is characterized by an increased PR interval and shortening of the QT interval. Tall, symmetric, peaked T waves are visible initially.

claims.text: Potassium > 6.5 mEq/L: the QRS widens and P waves disappear.
claims.quote: Potassium > 6.5 mEq/L (> 6.5 mmol/L) causes further slowing of conduction with widening of the QRS interval, disappearance of the P wave

claims.text: Hypokalemia: get an ECG for moderate to severe cases. Cardiac effects are usually minimal until potassium drops below 3 mEq/L.
claims.quote: ECG should be done on patients with moderate to severe hypokalemia. Cardiac effects of hypokalemia are usually minimal until serum potassium concentrations are < 3 mEq/L

claims.text: Hypokalemia can cause PVCs, PACs, ventricular and supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, and second- or third-degree AV block.
claims.quote: Hypokalemia may cause premature ventricular beats and premature atrial contractions, ventricular and supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, and second- or third-degree atrioventricular block
